‘Dark showering’ is having a moment. Best enjoyed as a way of winding down in the evening, it entails opting for low lighting (including, in some cases, with an old-school lava lamp) and running the water cold enough to curl your toes. The idea is that you can lower your cortisol levels with something as simple as your daily shower—or so the thinking goes. There are some huge claims behind it. One user even maintains that taking 30-second showers can “reprogram your subconscious.” But what do doctors say?

blocks.x: According to Dr. Naomi Murphy, a psychologist at Octopus Psychology, the low-cortisol shower phenomenon draws heavily from the cold exposure trend popularized over a decade ago. Prominent proponents like Wim Hof advocated for diving into freezing lakes and running up snowy mountains scantily clad as a way of boosting the immune system and lowering stress hormones (which sounds counterintuitive, but more on that below). Dark showering is a bit more user-friendly, since you’re unlikely to suffer frostbite in your bathroom.

Murphy says there’s actually something to low-cortisol showers, just not quite to the degree that TikTok claims. “The shock of the cold water does activate the sympathetic nervous system, causing a temporary spike in some stress hormones,” she says. This sounds like the opposite of what we're going for here, but it’s the post-shower after-effect, when cortisol levels dip well below normal levels, that can be useful for managing stress.

The thing is, while showering in a dark room with a lava lamp might be aesthetically appealing, Dr. Cynthia Odogwu, a physician at Kambili Health, says the dip in cortisol might not happen until hours later—by which time you might already be asleep. But Murphy adds that those with heart conditions and people at risk of stroke should ditch the cold showers entirely, lest the shock to the system prove fatal.

blocks.x: Odogwu argues that the best way to actually lower cortisol is with a warm shower. She points to a study in the European Journal of Applied Physiology that found washing water at around 90 degrees Farenheit—considered ‘temperature neutral’—actually decreased cortisol levels in the blood by about 34 percent.

Unfortunately for the long-soakers out there, a hot bath may spike levels. “When water temperature reaches 39ºC or more, which is what we call hot water, we start to see a rise in cortisol levels,” she says. “This is because soaking in hot water, especially for a long time, causes the deep body temperature to go up, whereas a pleasant warm shower does not.” (That said, there are other health benefits to soaking in hot bodies of water.)

Whichever method you choose, dimming your lights is a welcome way to wind down. Spending time in the dark has been proven to lower stress by reducing sensory overload. It can also help with your circadian rhythm and help with sleep. “While more research is needed, incorporating scents such as lavender, playing soothing music, and setting up dim lighting are low-risk options that may help reduce stress,” Odogwu says.
So while the benefits of shower in the dark might actually be greatly exaggerated, taking a more intentional approach to your evening ablutions is never a bad step at the end of a stressful day.
A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.
